avocado.name: Avocado
avocado.nutrition: Loaded with healthy fats for brain development, plus folate and fiber.

serve.6: Offer thick spears (about the size of two adult fingers) of ripe avocado. Roll in a little ground flax or crushed baby cereal for grip. Mashed avocado on a preloaded spoon also works well.
serve.9: Cut into bite-size cubes for developing pincer grasp, or keep offering spears. Mash onto strips of toast.
serve.12: Serve diced, sliced, or mashed — on toast, in quesadillas, or straight with a fork.

banana.name: Banana
banana.nutrition: Easy energy with potassium and vitamin B6. Very ripe bananas are easiest to digest.

serve.6: Snap a ripe banana in half and leave some peel on the bottom half as a natural handle, or cut into thick spears. Whole banana rounds are slippery — avoid coin shapes.
serve.9: Offer small bite-size pieces for pincer-grasp practice, or continue with spears.
serve.12: Sliced, whole (supervised), or mashed into oatmeal and yogurt.

apple.name: Apple
apple.nutrition: Fiber and vitamin C. Cooking softens it and makes nutrients easier to access.

serve.6: Steam or bake peeled apple halves or thick wedges until completely soft (a fork slides in easily). Serve warm wedges or mash into a chunky sauce.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size pieces, or finely grated raw apple. Unsweetened applesauce on a preloaded spoon.
serve.12: Continue cooked pieces or grated raw. Whole raw apple and thick raw slices remain choking hazards until at least age 4.

apple.hazardNote: Raw apple is a top choking hazard for babies and toddlers. Always cook until soft, grate raw, or slice paper-thin for older toddlers.

pear.name: Pear
pear.nutrition: Gentle on digestion with good fiber — helpful for constipation, common when starting solids.

serve.6: Very ripe, soft pear in thick wedges with skin removed, or steam firmer pears until soft. Mashed ripe pear works too.
serve.9: Soft ripe pear in bite-size pieces, or grated raw.
serve.12: Sliced ripe pear. Firm varieties still benefit from thin slicing or cooking.

pear.hazardNote: Firm pear poses a choking risk. Use very ripe, soft pears or cook until soft.

strawberry.name: Strawberry
strawberry.nutrition: Excellent vitamin C, which boosts iron absorption when served with iron-rich foods.

serve.6: Offer large, very ripe berries whole (bigger than a golf ball) for gnawing, or mash smaller ones into yogurt or oatmeal.
serve.9: Quarter or slice berries lengthwise for self-feeding with pincer grasp.
serve.12: Halved or quartered depending on size. Whole small berries remain a hazard until around age 4.

strawberry.hazardNote: Small round berries can block airways. Serve large berries whole only when soft and bigger than baby's mouth, otherwise slice or quarter.

blueberry.name: Blueberry
blueberry.nutrition: Antioxidant-rich with vitamin C and fiber.

serve.6: Squash each berry flat between your fingers, or stir mashed berries into oatmeal or yogurt.
serve.9: Flattened or halved berries for pincer-grasp practice.
serve.12: Halved berries. Whole blueberries become okay when chewing is strong, typically age 2+ with supervision.

blueberry.hazardNote: Whole blueberries are the classic size and shape to block a baby's airway. Always flatten or halve.

mango.name: Mango
mango.nutrition: Vitamins A and C for immune health and eyesight.

serve.6: Thick spears of ripe mango (slippery — a crinkle cutter or a roll in baby cereal helps). A large de-fleshed pit with some flesh attached makes a great teether under supervision.
serve.9: Bite-size cubes of ripe mango.
serve.12: Cubed or sliced, in yogurt, smoothies, or on its own.

peach.name: Peach
peach.nutrition: Vitamins A and C plus fiber.

serve.6: Very ripe peach halves (pit removed, skin on for grip) to gnaw, or thick soft wedges. Steam firm peaches until soft.
serve.9: Ripe peach in bite-size pieces, skin removed if it bothers baby.
serve.12: Sliced ripe peach.

peach.hazardNote: Firm peach flesh can break into hard chunks. Use very ripe fruit or cook until soft. Remove the pit.

orange.name: Orange
orange.nutrition: Classic vitamin C source — pairs beautifully with iron-rich meals.

serve.6: Offer a large peeled wheel with membrane pierced, or supremed segments (membrane removed) cut small. Citrus may cause harmless rash around the mouth.
serve.9: Small pieces of supremed segments.
serve.12: Segments with thin membrane are usually manageable; halve them if large.

orange.hazardNote: Membranes can be hard to manage. Remove seeds and tough membrane for young babies.

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.nutrition: Hydrating with vitamins A and C.

serve.6: Thick seedless spears or a large thin wide slice to gnaw. Remove every seed.
serve.9: Bite-size seedless pieces.
serve.12: Small triangles or cubes, seeds removed.

watermelon.hazardNote: Chunks can break off in hard pieces; remove all seeds.

grape.name: Grapes
grape.nutrition: Quick energy, vitamin K and hydration.

serve.6: Best to wait, or offer only as a smashed/quartered mash. Whole or halved grapes are never safe at this age.
serve.9: Quarter lengthwise (never crosswise into rounds). Skin can be peeled for younger eaters.
serve.12: Continue quartering lengthwise until at least age 4 — this is non-negotiable.

grape.hazardNote: Whole grapes are one of the top causes of fatal choking in young children. ALWAYS quarter lengthwise until at least age 4.

kiwi.name: Kiwi
kiwi.nutrition: More vitamin C per gram than oranges. Acidity may cause harmless mouth rash.

serve.6: Peel and cut into thick spears, or halve and let baby scoop with a spoon assist.
serve.9: Peeled, in bite-size pieces.
serve.12: Sliced or diced; some toddlers enjoy halved kiwi with a spoon.

cherry.name: Cherries
cherry.nutrition: Antioxidants and a little melatonin — some families swear by better naps.

serve.6: Pit and mash, or chop finely and stir into yogurt or oatmeal.
serve.9: Pitted and quartered.
serve.12: Pitted and halved or quartered until chewing is reliable (about age 4 for whole).

cherry.hazardNote: Round, firm, and slippery with a pit — a serious choking hazard whole. Always pit and quarter or chop.

sweet-potato.name: Sweet Potato
sweet-potato.nutrition: Beta-carotene (vitamin A) powerhouse for eyes and immunity. Naturally sweet — an easy early win.

serve.6: Roast or steam skin-on wedges until very soft, then remove skin. Thick spears baby can palm, or mash on a preloaded spoon.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size cubes, or continue wedges.
serve.12: Cubes, wedges, mash — or baked whole and scooped.

broccoli.name: Broccoli
broccoli.nutrition: Vitamin C, vitamin K, folate and fiber. The floret shape is nature's baby handle.

serve.6: Steam whole florets with a long stem until soft. Baby holds the stem and gnaws the floret — a perfect natural handle.
serve.9: Smaller soft-cooked florets or bite-size pieces.
serve.12: Bite-size cooked pieces; try roasted with olive oil and a squeeze of lemon.

carrot.name: Carrot
carrot.nutrition: Beta-carotene for vision and immune health.

serve.6: Steam or roast thick sticks or halved large carrots until a fork slides in easily. Mashed cooked carrot also works.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size pieces or continue soft sticks.
serve.12: Soft-cooked pieces, or finely grated raw. Raw sticks and coins stay off the menu until at least age 4.

carrot.hazardNote: Raw carrot is a top choking hazard. Always cook until soft, or grate raw for toddlers.

peas.name: Peas
peas.nutrition: Plant protein, iron, and fiber in a tiny package.

serve.6: Mash or flatten cooked peas, or blend into a chunky mash on a preloaded spoon.
serve.9: Whole cooked peas are generally fine now and excellent pincer practice — flatten them if you want extra caution.
serve.12: Whole cooked peas, in pasta, rice, or straight off the tray.

peas.hazardNote: Small and round — flatten or mash for young babies.

serve.6: Steam whole beans until very soft — the long shape is easy to hold and gnaw.
serve.9: Soft-cooked beans cut into small pieces, or continue whole soft beans.
serve.12: Cooked pieces; roasted green beans make a great finger food.

zucchini.name: Zucchini
zucchini.nutrition: Mild, hydrating, and easy to cook soft — a low-stress early vegetable.

serve.6: Steam or roast thick spears (skin on for grip) until soft.
serve.9: Soft-cooked half-moons or bite-size pieces.
serve.12: Cooked pieces, grated into fritters, or ribboned into pasta.

butternut-squash.name: Butternut Squash
butternut-squash.nutrition: Beta-carotene and vitamin C with a naturally sweet flavor babies love.

serve.6: Roast or steam wedges until very soft; serve thick spears or mash.
serve.9: Soft-cooked cubes.
serve.12: Cubes, mash, or blended into pasta sauce and soups.

potato.name: Potato
potato.nutrition: Energy, potassium and vitamin C. A neutral base for stronger flavors.

serve.6: Steamed or baked wedges, soft all the way through. Mashed potato (thin with breast milk or formula) on a preloaded spoon.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size pieces or small smashed potatoes.
serve.12: Any soft preparation — wedges, mash, shredded hash browns cooked soft.

cauliflower.name: Cauliflower
cauliflower.nutrition: Vitamin C and fiber; can cause some gas — normal and temporary.

serve.6: Steam whole florets with stems until soft; baby grips the stem.
serve.9: Small soft-cooked florets or pieces.
serve.12: Roasted florets, riced cauliflower, or in cheese sauce.

spinach.name: Spinach
spinach.nutrition: Iron, folate and vitamin K. Pair with vitamin C foods to boost iron absorption.

serve.6: Finely chop cooked spinach and fold into scrambled egg yolk, oatmeal, or mashed vegetables. Raw leaves can stick to the palate — cook it.
serve.9: Chopped cooked spinach in eggs, pasta, fritters, or yogurt dips.
serve.12: Cooked and chopped in almost anything; some toddlers accept small raw leaves torn up.

tomato.name: Tomato
tomato.nutrition: Vitamin C and lycopene. Acidity can cause harmless rash around the mouth.

serve.6: Large tomato wedges (seeds okay), or quartered cherry tomatoes. Low-sodium tomato sauce on pasta is great too.
serve.9: Quartered cherry tomatoes or diced large tomato.
serve.12: Diced tomato; keep quartering cherry tomatoes until at least age 4.

tomato.hazardNote: Cherry and grape tomatoes are round choking hazards — always quarter lengthwise.

cucumber.name: Cucumber
cucumber.nutrition: Mostly water — hydrating and soothing for teething gums (try it cold).

serve.6: A thick, long spear with skin on for grip (baby gnaws, doesn't really eat much) — stay close. Cold cucumber soothes gums.
serve.9: Thin ribbons (use a peeler) or small thin slices.
serve.12: Thin slices or quartered spears. Avoid thick coins until chewing is reliable.

cucumber.hazardNote: Firm raw chunks and coins are risky. Use large spears for gnawing or thin ribbons.

corn.name: Corn

serve.6: Cooked corn on the cob (halved crosswise) — baby gnaws kernels off, which is safer than loose kernels. Or blend kernels into a mash.
serve.9: Loose cooked kernels are usually okay now; flatten them for extra caution.
serve.12: On the cob or loose kernels.

corn.hazardNote: Loose kernels can be inhaled by young babies; on the cob is safer early on.

beet.name: Beets
beet.nutrition: Folate and antioxidants. Heads up: red beets turn diapers pink — harmless!

serve.6: Roast or steam until very soft; serve thick wedges or mash.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size pieces (expect glorious mess).
serve.12: Cooked pieces or grated raw in small amounts.

beet.hazardNote: Raw or undercooked beet is hard and risky — cook until completely soft.

bell-pepper.name: Bell Pepper
bell-pepper.nutrition: One of the best vitamin C sources in the produce aisle.

serve.6: Roast or steam wide strips until soft, skin removed if tough.
serve.9: Soft-cooked small pieces, or very thin raw strips to gnaw.
serve.12: Thin raw strips or cooked pieces.

bell-pepper.hazardNote: Raw pepper is firm and the skin is slippery. Cook soft for babies; thin raw strips for toddlers.

mushroom.name: Mushrooms
mushroom.nutrition: B vitamins, selenium, and vitamin D when UV-exposed.

serve.6: Cook well (sautéed or roasted until tender) and chop finely into eggs, pasta, or mash.
serve.9: Well-cooked, chopped small.
serve.12: Cooked slices or quarters.

mushroom.hazardNote: Rubbery texture is hard to chew — cook well and chop.

egg.name: Egg
egg.nutrition: Nearly a complete food: protein, choline for brain development, iron, and vitamin D.

serve.6: Introduce early and keep it regular — early introduction may reduce allergy risk. Serve a well-cooked omelet cut into strips, or hard-boiled egg mashed with a little water, breast milk, or formula.
serve.9: Scrambled egg pieces, omelet strips, or quartered hard-boiled eggs.
serve.12: Any fully-cooked style: scrambled, boiled, egg cups, French toast fingers.

chicken.name: Chicken
chicken.nutrition: Protein, iron and zinc — dark meat (thigh) has more iron and stays moister.

serve.6: A whole cooked drumstick (skin, cartilage and loose bone fragments removed) makes a natural handle — baby gnaws and sucks. Or finely shredded moist thigh meat, or blended chicken folded into mash.
serve.9: Finely shredded or thin small strips of moist chicken; meatballs made soft with breadcrumbs.
serve.12: Shredded, diced, or soft meatballs. Avoid tough dry chunks.

chicken.hazardNote: Dry, crumbly chunks are hard to manage. Keep it moist; shred or serve large pieces to gnaw.

beef.name: Beef
beef.nutrition: One of the best iron sources for babies — heme iron absorbs far better than plant iron.

serve.6: A large strip of soft-cooked steak to hold and suck the juices (baby gnaws, swallows little), or well-cooked ground beef mixed into mash. Slow-cooked shredded beef is ideal.
serve.9: Ground beef, soft meatballs, or finely shredded slow-cooked beef.
serve.12: Small tender pieces, meatballs, bolognese, or shredded beef tacos.

beef.hazardNote: Chunks of steak are a hazard. Serve as a large piece to suck/gnaw, or ground and soft.

salmon.name: Salmon
salmon.nutrition: Omega-3 DHA for brain and eye development, plus protein, iron and vitamin D.

serve.6: Cooked salmon flaked and checked meticulously for bones, served in small clumps or mixed into mash or avocado. Introduce early — fish is a common allergen.
serve.9: Flaked salmon, salmon patties, or small pieces.
serve.12: Flaked fillet, salmon cakes, or mixed into pasta and rice.

white-fish.name: White Fish (Cod)
white-fish.nutrition: Mild, lean protein with B12 and selenium — a gentle first fish.

serve.6: Poach or bake, check thoroughly for bones, and flake into soft clumps or fold into mashed potato.
serve.9: Flaked pieces or soft fish cakes.
serve.12: Flaked fish, fish cakes, or homemade fish fingers (baked soft).

shrimp.name: Shrimp
shrimp.nutrition: Lean protein with iodine, selenium and B12. Shellfish is a common allergen — introduce deliberately.

serve.6: Cook well and chop very finely, mixed into mash, congee, or scrambled eggs.
serve.9: Finely chopped cooked shrimp.
serve.12: Small pieces of well-cooked shrimp (halve lengthwise, then chop).

shrimp.hazardNote: Rubbery texture — chop finely for young babies.

turkey.name: Turkey
turkey.nutrition: Protein, iron and zinc, similar to chicken; dark meat is richer in iron.

serve.6: Moist shredded thigh meat, or soft turkey meatballs mashed into pieces. Ground turkey folded into vegetable mash works well.
serve.9: Soft meatballs, ground turkey, or fine shreds.
serve.12: Meatballs, patties, shredded or diced moist turkey.

turkey.hazardNote: Dry turkey is crumbly and hard to manage. Keep it moist; thighs over breast.

pork.name: Pork

serve.6: Slow-cooked pork shredded finely, or a large strip of tender pork to gnaw. Avoid processed pork (bacon, sausage) — very high sodium.
serve.9: Finely shredded pulled pork or soft ground-pork meatballs.
serve.12: Shredded or small tender pieces.

pork.hazardNote: Chops and dry chunks are tough. Slow-cooked and shredded is safest.

tofu.name: Tofu
tofu.nutrition: Plant protein, calcium and iron. Soy is a common allergen — introduce on purpose.

serve.6: Thick strips of firm tofu (roll in crushed cereal or hemp seeds for grip), or mashed silken tofu on a spoon.
serve.9: Cubes of firm tofu, plain or lightly pan-seared.
serve.12: Cubes, strips, scrambled tofu, or in soups.

liver.name: Chicken Liver
liver.nutrition: The single richest common source of iron and vitamin A. Serve small amounts about once a week — vitamin A is potent.

serve.6: Cook thoroughly and mash into a smooth pâté; spread thinly on toast strips or stir a spoonful into vegetable mash.
serve.9: Pâté on toast strips, or small soft pieces mixed into other foods.
serve.12: Pâté, or blended into meatballs and bolognese.

oats.name: Oatmeal
oats.nutrition: Fiber, plant iron (choose fortified baby oatmeal for more), and steady energy.

serve.6: Thick oatmeal on a preloaded spoon, or so thick baby can grab handfuls. Mix with mashed fruit, breast milk, or formula.
serve.9: Thick oatmeal for spoon practice; baked oatmeal fingers for self-feeding.
serve.12: Any style — porridge, overnight oats, oat pancakes.

bread.name: Bread & Toast
bread.nutrition: Choose low-sodium, whole-grain bread. Wheat is a common allergen — introduce deliberately.

serve.6: Lightly toasted strips topped with a thin spread (avocado, hummus, thinned nut butter). Avoid untoasted fluffy bread.
serve.9: Toast strips or small pieces with spreads.
serve.12: Toast, sandwiches cut into strips, pita triangles.

bread.hazardNote: Fresh soft bread can gum into a sticky ball. Lightly toast it for babies.

pasta.name: Pasta
pasta.nutrition: Energy and (if fortified) B vitamins and iron. A friendly vehicle for sauces, fish and vegetables.

serve.6: Large shapes cooked very soft: fusilli, rigatoni, or thick strips of lasagna sheet. Toss with olive oil or low-sodium sauce.
serve.9: Cooked-soft shapes of any size; cut long noodles.
serve.12: Any pasta, any sauce (watch sodium in jarred sauces).

rice.name: Rice
rice.nutrition: Gentle energy. Vary grains (oats, barley, quinoa) to limit arsenic exposure from rice.

serve.6: Cook sticky/overcooked so it clumps — baby grabs handfuls. Congee (rice porridge) on a preloaded spoon is perfect.
serve.9: Sticky rice clumps, rice balls, or spoon-fed congee.
serve.12: Regular rice with meals.

quinoa.name: Quinoa
quinoa.nutrition: A complete plant protein with iron and fiber.

serve.6: Cook until very soft and fold into mash, yogurt, or thick porridge — the grains are too small to pick up alone.
serve.9: Quinoa mixed into soft foods, or formed into small baked patties.
serve.12: As a side grain, in bowls and salads.

pancake.name: Pancakes
pancake.nutrition: A perfect vehicle: fold in banana, ricotta, spinach, or ground flax. Skip syrup for babies.

serve.6: Soft, thin pancake strips (about two adult fingers wide). Sweeten with mashed banana, not sugar or honey (no honey before 12 months).
serve.9: Strips or small pieces.
serve.12: Quartered or whole small pancakes. Honey is okay now (after the first birthday).

yogurt.name: Yogurt
yogurt.nutrition: Protein, calcium, and probiotics. Choose plain whole-milk yogurt — flavored ones are sugar bombs.

serve.6: Plain whole-milk yogurt on a preloaded spoon, or let baby dive in with hands (embrace the mess). Stir in mashed fruit.
serve.9: Spoon practice with thick yogurt; use as a dip for fruit and toast.
serve.12: Yogurt with fruit, in smoothies, as a dip base.

cheese.name: Cheese
cheese.nutrition: Calcium, protein and fat. Pick low-sodium options: fresh mozzarella, ricotta, Swiss.

serve.6: Thin strips of fresh mozzarella, ricotta spread on toast, or melted into vegetables. Skip high-sodium cheeses most days.
serve.9: Shredded cheese, thin slices, ricotta by the spoon.
serve.12: Shreds, thin slices, melted — avoid cubes until chewing is strong.

cheese.hazardNote: Cubes and chunks of firm cheese are choking hazards. Serve thin slices, shreds, or melted.

butter.name: Butter & Ghee
butter.nutrition: Energy-dense fat that helps absorb vitamins A, D, E and K. Use unsalted.

serve.6: Melt a little unsalted butter into vegetables, oatmeal, or eggs — adds calories and flavor.
serve.9: Same — a cooking fat and flavor booster.
serve.12: Spread thinly on toast; cook with it freely.

cottage-cheese.name: Cottage Cheese
cottage-cheese.nutrition: Very high protein. Look for low-sodium versions for babies.

serve.6: Low-sodium cottage cheese on a preloaded spoon or mixed with mashed fruit.
serve.9: By the spoonful, or as a dip/topping on toast strips.
serve.12: With fruit, on toast, in pancake batter.

lentils.name: Lentils
lentils.nutrition: Plant iron, protein, folate and fiber. Pair with vitamin C for better iron absorption.

serve.6: Cook until very soft (red lentils collapse nicely) and serve as thick dal on a preloaded spoon, or fold into mash.
serve.9: Thick lentil stews, lentil patties, or mixed into rice.
serve.12: Dal, soups, patties — lentils in any form.

chickpeas.name: Chickpeas

serve.6: Smooth hummus (low-sodium, no whole seeds) spread on toast strips, or well-cooked chickpeas mashed thoroughly.
serve.9: Flattened/smashed chickpeas for pincer practice; hummus as a dip.
serve.12: Smashed or halved chickpeas; whole soft-cooked around 18mo+ with good chewing.

chickpeas.hazardNote: Whole chickpeas are round and firm — always smash or mash for babies.

black-beans.name: Black Beans

serve.6: Mash well-cooked (low-sodium) beans into a paste; spread on toast or mix into avocado.
serve.9: Flattened whole beans for finger practice, or mashed.
serve.12: Whole soft beans, bean quesadillas, soups.

black-beans.hazardNote: Whole beans can be a hazard for young babies — flatten or mash at first.

edamame.name: Edamame
edamame.nutrition: Complete plant protein with iron and folate.

serve.6: Best mashed into a smooth paste or blended into purees at this age.
serve.9: Smashed flat or finely chopped, shelled only.
serve.12: Halved or smashed shelled beans; whole around age 2+ with strong chewing.

edamame.hazardNote: Firm, round and smooth — a real choking hazard whole. Always smash or chop; never serve in the pod to babies.

peanut-butter.name: Peanut Butter
peanut-butter.nutrition: Early, regular peanut introduction is linked to dramatically lower allergy risk (LEAP study). Protein, healthy fat, niacin.

serve.6: Thin smooth peanut butter with warm water, breast milk or formula into a drizzle; stir into oatmeal or yogurt, or spread paper-thin on toast. Never by the spoonful, never chunky.
serve.9: Thinly spread on toast strips or mixed into foods, several times a week to maintain tolerance.
serve.12: Thin spreads and mixed into foods. Whole peanuts remain off-limits until at least age 4.

peanut-butter.hazardNote: Thick glops of nut butter can block airways, and whole peanuts are unsafe until age 4+. Always thin it or spread thinly.

almond-butter.name: Almond Butter
almond-butter.nutrition: Vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fats. Tree nuts are a common allergen — introduce one at a time.

serve.6: Thin smooth almond butter into oatmeal, yogurt, or a paper-thin toast spread.
serve.9: Thin spreads and mix-ins, offered regularly.
serve.12: Thin spreads; finely ground almonds in baking. No whole nuts until 4+.

almond-butter.hazardNote: Same rules as peanut butter: thin it out or spread paper-thin. Whole almonds are unsafe until age 4+.

tahini.name: Tahini (Sesame)
tahini.nutrition: Sesame is a top-9 allergen worth introducing early. Tahini brings calcium, iron and healthy fat.

serve.6: Thin with water and drizzle over vegetables, stir into yogurt, or serve as hummus.
serve.9: Thinned drizzles, hummus, tahini-yogurt dips.
serve.12: In dressings, dips and baking.

tahini.hazardNote: Thick paste can clump — thin it before serving.

chia.name: Chia Seeds
chia.nutrition: Omega-3 ALA, fiber, iron and calcium in a sprinkle.

serve.6: Stir a small spoonful into oatmeal or yogurt (they soften as they absorb liquid), or make chia pudding.
serve.9: Chia pudding, sprinkled into porridge and smoothies.
serve.12: Puddings, smoothies, baked into muffins.

flax.name: Ground Flaxseed
flax.nutrition: Omega-3 ALA and fiber. Always ground — whole seeds pass through undigested.

serve.6: Sprinkle ground flax into oatmeal, yogurt, or use it to add grip to slippery foods like avocado and banana.
serve.9: Mixed into porridge, baking, and smoothies.
serve.12: Same — a daily sprinkle habit is an easy win.

raspberry.name: Raspberries
raspberry.nutrition: Fiber champion of the berry world, with vitamin C and antioxidants.

serve.6: Soft enough to serve whole if large and ripe — or flatten each berry between your fingers. Mash into yogurt or oatmeal.
serve.9: Whole ripe berries (flattened if firm) for pincer practice.
serve.12: Whole or halved berries.

blackberry.name: Blackberries
blackberry.nutrition: Vitamin C, vitamin K and fiber.

serve.6: Halve lengthwise or smash; fold mashed berries into oatmeal or yogurt.
serve.9: Halved or flattened berries.
serve.12: Halved berries; whole once chewing is strong.

blackberry.hazardNote: Large firm blackberries can be a hazard — halve or flatten them.

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.nutrition: Vitamin C and manganese, plus bromelain (why your tongue tingles).

serve.6: A large thin ring or long thin spear of very ripe pineapple to gnaw, or finely chopped into yogurt.
serve.9: Small thin pieces of ripe pineapple.
serve.12: Bite-size pieces.

pineapple.hazardNote: Fibrous and firm — serve thin, small or very ripe. Acidity can cause harmless mouth rash.

cantaloupe.name: Cantaloupe
cantaloupe.nutrition: Beta-carotene and vitamin C in a hydrating package.

serve.6: Thin wide slices of ripe melon (rind removed) or thick spears soft enough to smash between your fingers.
serve.9: Small bite-size pieces of ripe melon.
serve.12: Cubes or small wedges.

cantaloupe.hazardNote: Firm melon chunks can break off in hard pieces — use ripe melon, sliced thin.

plum.name: Plum
plum.nutrition: Fiber and sorbitol — a gentle constipation helper.

serve.6: Very ripe plum halves (pit removed, skin on for grip) to gnaw, or steam firm plums until soft.
serve.9: Ripe plum in bite-size pieces.
serve.12: Sliced ripe plum.

plum.hazardNote: Remove the pit; firm plums need cooking or very thin slicing.

apricot.name: Apricot
apricot.nutrition: Beta-carotene and fiber; dried apricots are iron-dense (chop well).

serve.6: Very ripe apricot halves, pit removed, or steamed until soft and mashed.
serve.9: Ripe pieces; finely chopped dried apricot softened in warm water.
serve.12: Sliced fresh, or finely chopped dried apricots.

apricot.hazardNote: Remove the pit. Dried apricots are sticky and chewy — chop finely if offered.

papaya.name: Papaya
papaya.nutrition: Vitamin C, folate and digestive enzymes — famously gentle on tummies.

serve.6: Thick spears of ripe papaya (roll in ground flax for grip) or mashed.
serve.9: Bite-size cubes of ripe papaya.
serve.12: Cubed or sliced.

fig.name: Figs
fig.nutrition: Fiber, calcium and potassium; dried figs are concentrated sugar — fresh is better for babies.

serve.6: Quarter a ripe fresh fig lengthwise, or mash the flesh into oatmeal.
serve.9: Quartered fresh figs or small pieces.
serve.12: Halved or quartered fresh figs; finely chopped dried figs.

coconut.name: Coconut
coconut.nutrition: Rich fats for energy. Coconut milk and yogurt are great dairy-free bases.

serve.6: Stir unsweetened coconut milk into oatmeal and curries, or finely shredded coconut into porridge.
serve.9: Fine shreds mixed into food; coconut yogurt.
serve.12: Shredded coconut on yogurt; small thin slivers of fresh coconut.

coconut.hazardNote: Raw coconut chunks are hard — use shredded, flaked or blended forms.

pomegranate.name: Pomegranate

serve.6: Best to wait, or offer only juice-crushed arils stirred into yogurt (seeds crushed flat).
serve.9: Crush each aril between your fingers before serving, or chop into yogurt.
serve.12: Crushed or halved arils; whole arils only when chewing is reliable (age 3–4).

pomegranate.hazardNote: Arils are small, round, firm and slippery — crush them for babies and young toddlers.

asparagus.name: Asparagus
asparagus.nutrition: Folate, vitamin K and prebiotic fiber (may make diapers smell funny — harmless).

serve.6: Steam or roast thick spears until completely soft; baby holds the stalk and gnaws the tip.
serve.9: Soft-cooked spears cut into small pieces.
serve.12: Cooked pieces or whole soft spears.

asparagus.hazardNote: The fibrous stalk can shred into strings — cook until fully soft and trim woody ends.

pumpkin.name: Pumpkin
pumpkin.nutrition: Beta-carotene, potassium and fiber, with a soft, spoonable texture.

serve.6: Roast or steam wedges until very soft; serve spears or mash. Plain canned pumpkin stirred into oatmeal works too.
serve.9: Soft-cooked cubes or thick pumpkin mash.
serve.12: Cubes, mash, pumpkin pancakes or muffins.

kale.name: Kale
kale.nutrition: Vitamin K, vitamin C, calcium and some iron.

serve.6: Cook until very tender and chop finely into eggs, mash, or blended sauces — raw leaves are too tough.
serve.9: Finely chopped cooked kale mixed into fritters, pasta, or scrambled eggs.
serve.12: Chopped cooked kale; crispy baked kale pieces for adventurous toddlers.

cabbage.name: Cabbage
cabbage.nutrition: Vitamin C and K, plus fiber. Expect some extra gas — normal.

serve.6: Steam or braise until silky-soft and chop finely into mash or grain dishes.
serve.9: Soft-cooked, finely chopped or thin soft ribbons.
serve.12: Cooked ribbons; small amounts of finely shredded raw cabbage in soft slaws.

brussels-sprouts.name: Brussels Sprouts
brussels-sprouts.nutrition: Vitamin C, vitamin K, folate and fiber.

serve.6: Steam or roast until very soft, then halve or quarter lengthwise.
serve.9: Quartered soft-cooked sprouts or chopped leaves.
serve.12: Halved roasted sprouts, cooked soft.

brussels-sprouts.hazardNote: Whole sprouts are round and firm — always halve or quarter and cook soft.

eggplant.name: Eggplant
eggplant.nutrition: Fiber and antioxidants; cooks down to a silky, easy-to-eat texture.

serve.6: Roast or steam thick spears until collapsing-soft (skin removed if tough), or mash into baba ganoush-style dip.
serve.9: Soft-cooked pieces or eggplant dip on toast strips.
serve.12: Cooked pieces, in pasta or curries.

onion.name: Onion
onion.nutrition: Prebiotic fiber and flavor-building — teaches baby real food tastes.

serve.6: Cook until fully soft and sweet (sautéed or roasted) and mix into any dish — rarely served alone.
serve.9: Well-cooked soft onion in eggs, sauces and stews.
serve.12: Cooked onion in anything; caramelized onion is usually a hit.

garlic.name: Garlic
garlic.nutrition: Flavor and immune-supporting compounds. Babies can love garlic — season their food!

serve.6: Cooked into dishes — sautéed with vegetables, in sauces, or roasted and mashed into spreads.
serve.9: Same — a seasoning, not a solo food.
serve.12: Cooked into family meals; roasted garlic spread on toast.

celery.name: Celery
celery.nutrition: Hydrating with vitamin K; mostly a texture-and-flavor food.

serve.6: Best finely chopped and cooked soft into soups, stews and sauces.
serve.9: Soft-cooked, de-stringed small pieces in mixed dishes.
serve.12: Cooked pieces. Raw celery sticks stay off the menu until at least age 4.

celery.hazardNote: Raw celery is a classic choking hazard: hard, fibrous and stringy. Cook soft and de-string for babies.

okra.name: Okra
okra.nutrition: Fiber, vitamin C and folate; the natural sliminess actually helps babies swallow.

serve.6: Steam or stew whole pods until soft; baby holds the pod and gnaws (remove the stem cap).
serve.9: Soft-cooked slices or chopped stewed okra.
serve.12: Stewed, roasted, or in gumbo-style dishes.

parsnip.name: Parsnip
parsnip.nutrition: Naturally sweet with fiber, folate and vitamin C.

serve.6: Roast or steam thick sticks until very soft, or mash with butter.
serve.9: Soft-cooked bite-size pieces or continue soft sticks.
serve.12: Roasted pieces or mash.

parsnip.hazardNote: Like carrot: hard when raw or undercooked. Cook until a fork slides through.

lamb.name: Lamb
lamb.nutrition: Exceptional iron and zinc — one of the best first meats.

serve.6: A large strip of slow-cooked lamb to hold and suck, or finely shredded/ground lamb folded into mash.
serve.9: Ground lamb, soft meatballs or fine shreds.
serve.12: Small tender pieces, koftas, or shredded slow-cooked lamb.

lamb.hazardNote: Chunks are tough — serve slow-cooked and shredded, ground, or as a large strip to gnaw.

sardines.name: Sardines
sardines.nutrition: Omega-3s, calcium, iron, vitamin D — tiny fish, huge nutrition, and very low mercury.

serve.6: Mash canned sardines (in water, low-sodium) thoroughly, remove the spine, and spread on toast strips or mix into mash.
serve.9: Mashed or flaked sardines, sardine cakes.
serve.12: Flaked sardines on toast or pasta.

sardines.hazardNote: Check for larger bones; the soft tiny bones in canned sardines are safe and full of calcium.

tuna.name: Tuna
tuna.nutrition: Protein and omega-3s. Choose light/skipjack tuna and keep to about once a week — albacore carries more mercury.

serve.6: Mash canned light tuna (in water, no salt added) with avocado, yogurt or olive oil until moist and clumpy.
serve.9: Moist flaked tuna, tuna patties, or tuna-avocado mash on toast.
serve.12: Tuna salad, patties, or flaked into pasta.

crab.name: Crab
crab.nutrition: Lean protein with zinc and B12. Shellfish allergen — introduce deliberately. Use real cooked crab, not imitation (high sodium).

serve.6: Shred cooked crab meat finely (check for shell fragments) and mix into congee, mash or scrambled egg.
serve.9: Finely shredded crab in mixed dishes or soft crab cakes.
serve.12: Crab cakes or shredded crab.

duck.name: Duck
duck.nutrition: Richer in iron than chicken, with plenty of healthy fat.

serve.6: Slow-roasted duck finely shredded (skin removed) and folded into mash or rice.
serve.9: Moist shredded duck or small soft pieces.
serve.12: Shredded or diced tender duck.

duck.hazardNote: Serve moist and shredded — dry slices are hard to manage.

tempeh.name: Tempeh
tempeh.nutrition: Fermented soy with protein, iron and probiotics; firmer and nuttier than tofu.

serve.6: Steam or simmer thick strips until soft (simmering mellows bitterness), or crumble finely into sauces.
serve.9: Soft-cooked strips or crumbles in mixed dishes.
serve.12: Pan-seared strips or crumbles in tacos and stir-fries.

barley.name: Barley
barley.nutrition: Chewy whole grain with beta-glucan fiber. Contains gluten.

serve.6: Cook pearl barley until very soft and fold into thick soups or mash — grains are too small to pick up alone.
serve.9: Soft-cooked barley in stews and grain bowls.
serve.12: Barley in soups, salads and pilafs.

millet.name: Millet
millet.nutrition: Gluten-free grain with iron, magnesium and B vitamins.

serve.6: Cook into a soft porridge (like polenta) and serve on a preloaded spoon or as set, cooled wedges.
serve.9: Millet porridge, or millet cooked sticky and formed into small balls.
serve.12: Fluffy millet as a side, or porridge with fruit.

couscous.name: Couscous
couscous.nutrition: Quick-cooking wheat pasta in tiny form. Whole-wheat versions add fiber.

serve.6: Cook soft and moisten with olive oil or sauce so it clumps; baby scoops handfuls. Pearl couscous is easier to pick up.
serve.9: Moist couscous clumps or pearl couscous pieces.
serve.12: As a side, in salads and bowls.

polenta.name: Polenta
polenta.nutrition: Gluten-free cornmeal comfort food; fortified versions add iron and B vitamins.

serve.6: Soft warm polenta on a preloaded spoon, or chill until set and cut into soft strips.
serve.9: Set polenta fingers, lightly pan-warmed, or creamy polenta with spoon practice.
serve.12: Creamy polenta, polenta fries (baked soft), or under sauces.

buckwheat.name: Buckwheat
buckwheat.nutrition: Despite the name, gluten-free and not wheat — a seed with complete protein, iron and magnesium.

serve.6: Cook groats until very soft into porridge, or make soft buckwheat pancake strips.
serve.9: Soft kasha (cooked groats) in mixed dishes; pancake pieces.
serve.12: Buckwheat pancakes, kasha, soba noodles cut up.

tortilla.name: Tortilla
tortilla.nutrition: Corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free; flour tortillas count as a wheat exposure. Watch sodium.

serve.6: Warm a low-sodium tortilla, spread with mashed avocado or hummus, roll tight and slice into pinwheel strips.
serve.9: Quesadilla strips with melted cheese and mashed beans.
serve.12: Small soft tacos, quesadilla triangles, pinwheels.

tortilla.hazardNote: Dry tortilla can gum into a wad — soften with a moist filling or warm it.

kefir.name: Kefir
kefir.nutrition: Drinkable yogurt with even more probiotic diversity. Choose plain, whole-milk kefir.

serve.6: A splash in an open cup with help, stirred into oatmeal, or blended with fruit into a spoonable smoothie.
serve.9: Open-cup or straw-cup practice with small amounts; smoothie bowls.
serve.12: Small cups of plain kefir or fruit-blended kefir.

ricotta.name: Ricotta
ricotta.nutrition: Soft, naturally lower-sodium cheese with protein and calcium.

serve.6: Spread on toast strips, dollop on a preloaded spoon, or fold into scrambled eggs and pasta.
serve.9: On toast, stirred into pasta, or by the spoonful.
serve.12: Ricotta pancakes, on toast with fruit, in lasagna.

paneer.name: Paneer
paneer.nutrition: Fresh, unsalted Indian cheese — high protein and naturally low sodium.

serve.6: Soft-simmered thin strips (curries soften it beautifully), or crumbled into mash.
serve.9: Crumbled paneer or thin soft-cooked strips.
serve.12: Cubes simmered soft in mild curries, or thin pan-seared strips.

paneer.hazardNote: Firm cubes can be a hazard — serve thin strips or crumbles, cooked soft.

white-beans.name: White Beans
white-beans.nutrition: Creamy cannellini and navy beans bring iron, protein, calcium and fiber.

serve.6: Mash low-sodium white beans with olive oil into a spread for toast strips, or fold into vegetable mash.
serve.9: Flattened whole beans for pincer practice, or white bean dip.
serve.12: Whole soft beans, in soups and pasta.

white-beans.hazardNote: Flatten or mash whole beans for young babies.

kidney-beans.name: Kidney Beans
kidney-beans.nutrition: Iron, protein and folate with a hearty texture.

serve.6: Mash well-cooked low-sodium kidney beans into a paste with a little olive oil or avocado.
serve.9: Flattened beans, or mashed into mild chili.
serve.12: Whole soft beans, mild chili, rice and beans.

kidney-beans.hazardNote: Flatten or mash for young babies. Always fully cooked (canned is fine) — never undercooked.

split-peas.name: Split Peas
split-peas.nutrition: Cook down into a naturally smooth, iron-rich porridge — zero prep hazards.

serve.6: Thick split pea dal or soup on a preloaded spoon, or thick enough to scoop by hand.
serve.9: Thick split pea stew with spoon practice; spread on toast.
serve.12: Split pea soup, dal with rice.

cashew-butter.name: Cashew Butter
cashew-butter.nutrition: A distinct tree-nut exposure from almond — introduce separately. Iron, zinc and magnesium.

serve.6: Thin smooth cashew butter with warm water into a drizzle for oatmeal or yogurt, or spread paper-thin on toast.
serve.9: Thin spreads and mix-ins, offered regularly.
serve.12: Thin spreads, cashew cream in sauces. No whole nuts until 4+.

cashew-butter.hazardNote: Same rules as all nut butters: thin it or spread paper-thin. Whole cashews unsafe until age 4+.

sunflower-butter.name: Sunflower Seed Butter
sunflower-butter.nutrition: Nut-free spread with vitamin E, iron and healthy fats — great for nut-allergic families.

serve.6: Thin with warm water and stir into oatmeal, or spread paper-thin on toast strips.
serve.9: Thin spreads and mix-ins.
serve.12: Thin spreads, in energy balls and baking.

sunflower-butter.hazardNote: Thick seed butters clump like nut butters — always thin or spread paper-thin.

hemp-seeds.name: Hemp Seeds
hemp-seeds.nutrition: Soft, tiny hearts with complete protein, iron, and omega-3s — no grinding needed.

serve.6: Sprinkle over yogurt and oatmeal, or use to add grip to slippery foods like banana and avocado.
serve.9: A daily sprinkle on almost anything.
serve.12: Sprinkled on meals, blended into smoothies.
